name: Henry Lau
languages: Spanish (from the California ranchos where he chained his first line)
equipment: Leather duster, brown, over a canvas surveyor's coat with a dozen pockets for pencils, tally pins and a pocket compass
Repeating rifle (Winchester, .44), 12 rounds in the magazine, issued by the survey for antelope and rattlesnakes
Hatchet for driving stakes and splitting kindling
A brass surveyor's transit in a fitted wooden case, the property of the Sweetwater & Big Horn Railway, which he cleans every night
A hundred-foot steel chain, tally pins and a striped range pole
His field books for the winter's survey, in a waxed canvas bag; Owen Lasker's handwriting is on half the pages
A tracing of the survey profile up Bitter Creek, made for his own use, with the Narrows marked 'Div. Pt.'
Horse: Plumb, a sorrel, steady and unhurried
A letter from his mother in Taishan, two years old and soft from reading, and $40 a month he sends home to her
features: Two Tongues (Immigrant origin: speaks Cantonese (Taishanese) and English fluently and one more language well; advantage on Insight and Perception checks to follow a conversation held in a language the speakers assume he doesn't know; among people who share one of his languages he finds a meal, a bed, work and the news without a check)

Trailcraft (Scout: never lost on terrain he has crossed or surveyed; finds water for himself, his companions and their horses each day without a check wherever any lies within a day's travel; follows a trail at a normal pace with a Survival check, learning how many riders, how long ago, and whether the horses were shod, loaded or lame)

Long Shot (Scout: attacking at long range with a Longarm doesn't impose disadvantage if he Aimed first this turn; his proficiency bonus is doubled for Perception checks to spot something more than 300 ft away; with his transit he can also give the exact range of anything he can see)

Ghost on the Range (Scout, 2nd level: in natural terrain he can Hide as a bonus action and can hide when only lightly obscured; travel pace doesn't impose disadvantage on his Stealth, and he leaves no trail that anyone without Trailcraft can follow unless he chooses)

Riding the Rails (Railroad Man background: railroad crews, telegraphers, surveyors and depot agents of every nation talk to him as one of their own; he knows how lines are located, graded and run, and the Sweetwater & Big Horn remembers him well)

personality.traits: I am precise about everything: distances, dates, money, promises. I listen far more than I talk. I have a dry, slow sense of humour that most people do not notice until a minute after the joke.
personality.ideals: A line is either true or it is not. So is a man. I would rather be thought rude than be thought a liar.
personality.bonds: The survey, and Mr. Wendt, who taught me the work and pays me what he pays a white instrument man. My mother in Taishan. And Owen Lasker, who shared my tent all winter, taught me cribbage, and never once called me anything but Henry.
personality.flaws: I have learned to be careful, and careful has sometimes meant silent when I should have spoken. I know things about the Narrows and about Owen that I have not told anyone, because nobody has asked, and because I do not know who in this valley I can trust.

appearance: A slight, upright man of twenty-eight with a calm, thoughtful face, short black hair under a wide felt hat, wire spectacles he wears for close work and pushes up for distance, and very clean hands with a pencil callus. Brown duster, a canvas coat full of pockets, a surveyor's transit case on his back.
backstory: Lau Hing, who has been Henry since a mission teacher in San Francisco gave him the name, was born in a village in Taishan county, Guangdong, in 1858, and came to California at nine with his uncle, who worked on the Central Pacific's crews in the Sierra and was killed in a snow slide in 1867. Henry was raised by his uncle's friends in Sacramento, went to a mission school, and at fifteen talked his way into carrying a range pole for a county surveyor who discovered that the boy could do trigonometry in his head. He has been a surveyor ever since: county roads, ranch boundaries in the San Joaquin, and since 1880 railroad location surveys across Nevada, Utah and Wyoming. In September 1885 he was working on a Union Pacific survey near Rock Springs, Wyoming, and what was done to the Chinese miners there that month is something he does not speak of; he left the Union Pacific's employ within the week. Horace Wendt hired him that winter as instrument man on the Sweetwater & Big Horn location survey, and he spent the winter in the foothill camp sharing a tent with the chainman, Owen Lasker. He knows that Owen was in the camp every day of the week of 10 April, because he signed the daily time book himself. He knows Owen copied the profile with the Narrows marked as the division point. And he knows Owen asked him, in March, what a man should do if he found out that a United States officer was taking money for other men's names.

dmNotes.roleplaying: Lau is the party's link to the railroad survey and its best witness on the facts that break the mystery: he signed the time book that proves the relinquishment forged (CLUE C2), he has a tracing of the profile (CLUE E1), and he heard Owen's question about 'a United States officer'. He joins the party when the survey arrives on the Sage Flats in bk-scenario-002, or earlier if the party rides into the foothills to find the survey camp in April. He is a fine scout and a calm marksman at long range, and his Long Shot and his transit's exact ranges make him valuable in the siege. He is careful with strangers and loyal to anyone who earns it. Treat him as a full person with his own politics: he wants the railroad built honestly, a fair wage, and his friend's killer found, and he has every reason to distrust Wyoming's courts and every intention of testifying anyway.
dmNotes.voice: Quiet, exact, educated English with a slight California lilt, every sentence finished. Uses numbers when other men use adjectives ('three hundred and forty yards', 'eleven days'). Dry humour, delivered deadpan. Speaks Cantonese to himself when he is working out a sum.
dmNotes.motivations: Primary: see Owen Lasker's killer found and tried, honestly. Secondary: keep his job, his transit and the survey's good name. Tertiary: send home enough money that his mother never has to wonder.
dmNotes.secrets: In March Owen told him the whole of it, without the name: that he had seen a letter proving that 'a United States officer in Gilead' was selling names to the Association, and that he meant to say so at the grange. Henry advised him to go to a judge, not the grange. He has blamed himself since, for not insisting. Second secret: in the survey's letter book he has seen the land department's March letter asking Wendt's opinion of 'the Narrows quarter, offered by Mr. G. Sayre, U.S. Commissioner'; he put the two together on the day he heard Owen was dead, and has told no one, because the man is a federal officer and Henry Lau is a Chinese surveyor in Wyoming eight months after Rock Springs. He will tell a party that has shown it can be trusted, and he will repeat it under oath to Judge Kittle.
dmNotes.attitude: Toward the party: polite, reserved, observant, warming steadily to those who treat him as an equal and abruptly cold to anyone who does not. Toward Horace Wendt: loyal, filial. Toward Thea Lasker: grave kindness; he brings her Owen's field books. Toward the Company's riders: wary, after they rode through the survey's stakes. Toward Gideon Sayre: polite, careful, and quietly certain.
